而旨趣之有遺或得其旨而詞華之不足此篇究
極明暢而敷貫沉雄當是文場老將練習於紀
律者也
考試官教諭劉批此題極難作盖欲發孤妍
於既枯求至味於不和非老手筆不能也此篇得之
===
考試官教諭吴批作論語題者直致則無華
強合則昧旨此篇詳贍當理足破羣疑
聖人言民心之公無古今之異明已之所以無毀譽
也盖好善惡惡無所私曲乃人心天理之同然聖人
豈有所毀譽自異於古今之人心哉且吾夫子既自
言於人無所毀譽矣至此復申言其故意謂世有古
今而人心之天理不殊人有古今而是非之公論常
在我之稱人之惡所以不敢損其真者誠以今日之
民即三代之時無有作惡之民所以惡其惡而無所
punctuated:
四書義

「斯民也，三代之所以直道而行也。」

劉實

同考試官教諭張批：論語一題，作者或達於詞而旨趣之有遺，或得其旨而詞華之不足。此篇究極明暢，而敷貫沉雄，當是文場老將練習於紀律者也。

考試官教諭劉批：此題極難作。盖欲發孤妍於既枯，求至味於不和，非老手筆不能也。此篇得之。

考試官教諭吴批：作論語題者，直致則無華，強合則昧旨。此篇詳贍當理，足破羣疑。

聖人言民心之公無古今之異，明已之所以無毀譽也。盖好善惡惡無所私曲，乃人心天理之同然，聖人豈有所毀譽自異於古今之人心哉？且吾夫子既自言於人無所毀譽矣，至此復申言其故。意謂：世有古今，而人心之天理不殊；人有古今，而是非之公論常在。我之稱人之惡，所以不敢損其真者，誠以今日之民，即三代之時無有作惡之民，所以惡其惡而無所
translation_en:
Expositions on the Four Books

"These people are those with whom the Three Dynasties walked the straight way."

Liu Shi 劉實

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Zhang 張: On this topic from the Analects (Lunyu 論語), writers either achieve fluency of expression while missing its underlying purport, or grasp the purport while lacking literary ornament. This essay is thoroughly clear and fluent, and its exposition is coherent, deep, and vigorous; the writer must be a veteran general of the examination halls who is well-practiced in the rules of composition.

Comment by Examiner Instructor Liu 劉: This topic is extremely difficult to compose upon. For to bring forth solitary beauty from what is already withered, and to seek the ultimate flavor in what is unblended, is impossible without the brush of a seasoned hand. This essay achieves it.

Comment by Examiner Instructor Wu 吳: Among those who write on topics from the Analects, being straightforward results in a lack of literary grace, while forcing connections obscures the meaning. This essay is detailed, rich, and true to principle—sufficient to dispel all doubts.

The Sage speaks of the impartiality of the people's minds having no difference between antiquity and the present, so as to clarify why he himself neither detracts nor overpraises. For loving the good and hating the bad without selfish bias or distortion is the common nature of the Heavenly Principle in the human mind; how could the Sage indulge in detraction or overpraise and thereby set himself apart from the minds of people past and present? Moreover, our Master, having already stated that toward others he neither detracts nor overpraises, at this point further explains the reason why. His meaning is that although ages are divided into past and present, the Heavenly Principle in the human mind does not differ; and although people belong to past and present, impartial judgment of right and wrong always endures. When I speak of a person's evil, the reason I dare not diminish the truth of it is truly because the people of today are the very people of the time of the Three Dynasties—people who indulged in no partiality of dislike, and with whom they therefore hated what was evil without any…

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
私曲也今日之民心惡惡以直道三代之民心惡惡
亦直道我豈得枉其惡惡之實而有所毀邪我之揚
人之善所以不敢過其實者亦以今此之民即三代
之時無有作好之民所以善其善而無所迂枉也今
此之民心好善以直道三代之民心好善亦直道我
豈得枉其善善之實而有所譽邪吾夫子言此盖不
以春秋衰世視此民而以三代盛時視此民可見矣
吁毀譽者一人之私心直道者萬世之公論不以一
人之私心而掩萬世之公論非聖人之至公至平疇
===
克爾哉抑考上文有曰如有所譽者其有所試矣則
雖無所毀而又有所譽不幾有所倚乎盖聖人樂道
人之善惡稱人之惡是以寧有先褒之善終無豫詆
之惡雖曰先褒亦必試其將然而不苟即書所謂與
其殺不辜寧失不經罪疑惟輕功疑惟重同一善善
速惡惡緩之意也豈曰有倚乎哉
衣錦尚絅惡其文之著也故君子之道闇然而
日章
李昕
punctuated:
私曲也。今日之民心惡惡以直道，三代之民心惡惡亦直道，我豈得枉其惡惡之實而有所毀邪？我之揚人之善，所以不敢過其實者，亦以今此之民，即三代之時無有作好之民，所以善其善而無所迂枉也。今此之民心好善以直道，三代之民心好善亦直道，我豈得枉其善善之實而有所譽邪？吾夫子言此，盖不以春秋衰世視此民，而以三代盛時視此民可見矣。吁！毀譽者，一人之私心；直道者，萬世之公論。不以一人之私心而掩萬世之公論，非聖人之至公至平，疇克爾哉？抑考上文有曰：「如有所譽者，其有所試矣。」則雖無所毀而又有所譽，不幾有所倚乎？盖聖人樂道人之善，惡稱人之惡，是以寧有先褒之善，終無豫詆之惡。雖曰先褒，亦必試其將然而不苟，即《書》所謂「與其殺不辜，寧失不經；罪疑惟輕，功疑惟重」，同一善善速、惡惡緩之意也，豈曰有倚乎哉？

「衣錦尚絅，惡其文之著也。故君子之道，闇然而日章。」
李昕
translation_en:
…selfish distortion. Since the minds of the people today hate evil in accordance with the straight way, just as the minds of the people of the Three Dynasties hated evil by the straight way, how could I distort the reality of what is hated as evil and engage in groundless detraction? And the reason that, in praising a person's goodness, I dare not exceed the reality is likewise because these people of today are the very people of the Three Dynasties who had no partiality in their likes, and who therefore approved of what was good without any crookedness or distortion. Since the minds of these people today love goodness in accordance with the straight way, just as the minds of the people of the Three Dynasties loved goodness by the straight way, how could I distort the reality of what is approved as good and engage in groundless overpraise? From our Master's speaking thus, it can be seen that he viewed these people not as those of the declining age of the Spring and Autumn period, but as those of the flourishing era of the Three Dynasties.

Alas! Detraction and overpraise are the selfish mind of a single individual; the straight way is the impartial judgment of ten thousand generations. Not to obscure the impartial judgment of ten thousand generations with the selfish mind of a single individual—were it not for the supreme impartiality and supreme fairness of the Sage, who could be capable of this? Yet if we examine the preceding text, which says, "If there is anyone whom I praise, there is a basis on which I have tested him," then even though there is no detraction, there is still praise—does this not come close to leaning to one side? This is because the Sage delights in speaking of people's goodness and dislikes speaking of people's evil; therefore, he would rather have goodness that is praised in advance, and never evil that is disparaged beforehand. And even when praising in advance, he must first test what the person will become and is never careless about it. This shares the exact same spirit of being quick to approve the good and slow to condemn the evil as what the Book of Documents (Shu) calls, "Rather than put to death an innocent person, you should run the risk of irregularity; in cases of doubtful crimes, deal with them lightly; in cases of doubtful merit, deal with them heavily." How could this be called leaning to one side?

"She over her embroidered robe puts on a plain single garment, because she dislikes the display of its elegance. Thus the Way of the noble man is unobtrusive, yet it daily becomes more illustrious." [Doctrine of the Mean 33.1]
By Li Xin 李昕.

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導陳批中庸題用心於內自著於
外乃朱子成言而學者不察遂至紛紛臆决茫無
定見此作其超然於倫輩者歟
考試官教諭劉批作此題者或以尚絅為為己
之心日章為為己之驗或以始則不欲其著於外終
則自有以著於外立說然皆不如用心於內自著於
外乃取朱子成語故特表而出之
考試官教諭吳批中庸義千篇一律此作獨異
於衆蓋非淺之為講學者
===
中庸既釋詩以見君子之學用心於內復申言以見
君子之道自著於外盖君子之學為己故常用心於
內然既有諸內豈不自著於外乎中庸於末章復自
下學立心之始而言首因詩辭從而釋之意謂衣錦
所以美其服而又尚之以絅者惡其文采之太著也
美服所以章其身而又襲之以衣者不欲華美之外
揚也是則君子之學惟欲自得故常用力於人所不
見初不事乎表暴焉君子之學務求成己故恒脩業
於人所不知初不志於烜耀焉豈非衣錦必尚絅歟
punctuated:
同考試官訓導陳批：《中庸》題「用心於內，自著於外」，乃朱子成言，而學者不察，遂至紛紛臆决，茫無定見。此作其超然於倫輩者歟！
考試官教諭劉批：作此題者，或以「尚絅」為為己之心、「日章」為為己之驗；或以始則不欲其著於外、終則自有以著於外立說。然皆不如「用心於內，自著於外」，乃取朱子成語，故特表而出之。
考試官教諭吳批：《中庸》義千篇一律，此作獨異於衆，蓋非淺之為講學者。
《中庸》既釋《詩》以見君子之學用心於內，復申言以見君子之道自著於外。盖君子之學為己，故常用心於內；然既有諸內，豈不自著於外乎？《中庸》於末章復自下學立心之始而言，首因《詩》辭從而釋之，意謂：「衣錦」所以美其服，而又尚之以絅者，惡其文采之太著也；美服所以章其身，而又襲之以衣者，不欲華美之外揚也。是則君子之學惟欲自得，故常用力於人所不見，初不事乎表暴焉；君子之學務求成己，故恒脩業於人所不知，初不志於烜耀焉。豈非衣錦必尚絅，斂…
translation_en:
Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Chen's comment: For this topic from the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong), "applying one's mind within, while naturally becoming manifest without" are the established words of Master Zhu [Zhu Xi]. Yet scholars fail to examine them, resulting in a jumble of conjectural judgments without any settled view. Is this composition not one that stands far above its peers!
Examiner and Instructor Liu's comment: Among those who write on this topic, some formulate their argument by taking "putting on a plain outer garment" as the mind of learning for oneself and "becoming daily more illustrious" as the verification of learning for oneself; others argue that at first one does not wish it to become manifest without, while in the end it naturally has that whereby it becomes manifest without. Yet none of these compare to "applying one's mind within, while naturally becoming manifest without," which draws upon Master Zhu's established words; therefore, we have specially singled it out for publication.
Examiner and Instructor Wu's comment: Expositions on the Doctrine of the Mean are a thousand pieces from the same mold, yet this composition alone differs from the crowd; clearly its author is no shallow student of the teachings.
After the Doctrine of the Mean explains the Odes (Shi) to show how the superior man in his learning applies his mind within, it further elaborates to show how the Way of the superior man naturally becomes manifest without. This is because the learning of the superior man is for the sake of himself, and so he constantly applies his mind within; yet once he possesses it within, how could it not naturally become manifest without? In its final chapter, the Doctrine of the Mean speaks again from the very beginning of how lower-level learning establishes its resolution. First, drawing upon the words of the Odes, it proceeds to explain them, meaning to say: "Wearing brocade" is the means to beautify one's attire, yet adding a plain outer garment over it is because one dislikes itspatterned brilliance being too conspicuous; fine clothing is the means to adorn one's person, yet covering it with an outer robe is because one does not wish its splendor to be displayed outwardly. Thus, the learning of the superior man seeks only self-realization, so he constantly exerts himself where others do not see, never from the outset engaging in outward display; the learning of the superior man strives to perfect himself, so he constantly cultivates his work where others do not know, never from the outset setting his ambition on dazzling prominence. Is this not a case of wearing brocade yet necessarily putting on a plain outer garment, drawing in [?]…

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
華以就實乎雖然君子之立心固如此然其道之著
見不可掩亦理勢之自然也故申言之若謂君子之
學雖曰惟欲自得不事表暴若闇然矣然美在其中
則有諸内者日形諸外故不求人知而人自知之君
子之學雖曰務求成己不志烜耀若暗昧矣然善有
諸己則積於此者日發於彼故不虞人譽而人自譽
之由是言之尚絅故闇然衣錦故有日章之實實理
自然之符驗焉可誣哉大抵此因前章極致之言子
思子恐學者求之高遠故言之如此下文遂及入德
===
之方謹獨之事馴致篤恭天下平其妙至於無聲無
臭則中庸之極功也先儒有言此章再叙入德成德
之序信夫
觀水有術必觀其瀾日月有明容光必照焉
鄭鴻
同考試官教諭張批孟子此節陳氏以為二
者皆於用處知其本諸作皆不能發惟此篇
得之
考試官教諭劉批此作理得而詞贍滿場
punctuated:
華以就實乎？雖然，君子之立心固如此，然其道之著見不可掩，亦理勢之自然也。故申言之，若謂君子之學雖曰惟欲自得，不事表暴，若闇然矣；然美在其中，則有諸内者日形諸外，故不求人知而人自知之。君子之學雖曰務求成己，不志烜耀，若暗昧矣；然善有諸己，則積於此者日發於彼，故不虞人譽而人自譽之。由是言之，尚絅故闇然，衣錦故有日章之實，實理自然之符驗，焉可誣哉！大抵此因前章極致之言，子思子恐學者求之高遠，故言之如此。下文遂及入德之方、謹獨之事，馴致篤恭天下平，其妙至於無聲無臭，則中庸之極功也。先儒有言：「此章再叙入德成德之序。」信夫！

「觀水有術，必觀其瀾。日月有明，容光必照焉。」
鄭鴻
同考試官教諭張批：孟子此節，陳氏以為二者皆於用處知其本，諸作皆不能發，惟此篇得之。
考試官教諭劉批：此作理得而詞贍，滿場
translation_en:
…outer ostentation in order to pursue what is genuine? Even so, although the gentleman establishes his mind in this way, the fact that his Way becomes manifest and cannot be concealed is also the natural course of principle and tendency. Therefore, the text elaborates upon it, as if to say: Although the learning of the gentleman seeks only self-realization and does not engage in outward display, thus appearing dark and obscure, yet because beauty lies within, what is possessed inside daily takes form on the outside; thus he does not seek to be known by others, and yet others naturally know him. Although the learning of the gentleman strives to perfect himself and does not aim at brilliant renown, thus appearing dim and hidden, yet because goodness is possessed in himself, what is accumulated here daily manifests itself there; thus he does not anticipate the praise of others, and yet others naturally praise him. Speaking from this perspective, because he wears a plain unlined garment over it, he appears obscure, and because he wears brocade beneath, there is the reality of daily becoming more illustrious. This is the natural verification of real principle—how could it be falsified? In general, because of the words on the ultimate perfection in the preceding chapter, Master Zisi feared that learners might seek it in what is lofty and distant, and therefore spoke of it like this. The text below then proceeds to the method of entering into virtue and the practice of being watchful over oneself when alone, gradually reaching the point where, through篤恭 (earnest and reverent composure), all under Heaven is brought to peace, its subtlety extending to having neither sound nor smell—which is the ultimate achievement of the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong). A former Confucian scholar said: "This chapter recounts once more the sequence of entering into virtue and perfecting virtue." Truly it is so!

"There is an art to contemplating water: one must contemplate its foaming waves. The sun and moon have brilliance: wherever a crack admits light, they necessarily shine into it."
Zheng Hong 鄭鴻
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Zhang: Regarding this passage of the Mencius (Mengzi), Mr. Chen held that in both cases one knows the root from its functioning. None of the other essays were able to bring this out; only this piece grasped it.
Comment by Examiner Instructor Liu: This composition grasps the principle and is rich in expression; in the entire examination hall…

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
所無
考試官教諭吳批孟子義詞氣秀發所
謂惟陳言之務去戛戛乎其難哉者歟
大賢即物以明聖道必於其用而知其本焉夫聖人
之道用易見而本難知苟不即水之瀾與日月之必
照以觀之抑何以知之哉何則流而為川瀦而為海
者水也人知水之混混而不知其有本也故觀水之
術不於歸會之所必於湍急之處則知其往過來續
而非朝滿夕除也不舍晝夜而非涸可立待也觀水
===
之瀾則知其源之有本如此若夫聖人之道發而為
小德川流無時不然者必有大德敦化者為之本焉
懸象於天代明晝夜者日月也人知日月之有明而
不知其有本也故觀日月之術不於物無遁形之間
必於容光必照之處則知其罅隙不遺而非明此暗
彼也無幽不燭而非大及小遺也觀日月於容光之
隙無不照則知其明之有本如此若夫聖人之道用
而為泛應曲當無物不有者必有一理渾然者為之
本焉然則聖道之大豈徒然而已哉抑嘗論之聖人
punctuated:
所無。
考試官教諭吳批：《孟子》義詞氣秀發，所謂「惟陳言之務去，戛戛乎其難哉」者歟！
大賢即物以明聖道，必於其用而知其本焉。夫聖人之道，用易見而本難知，苟不即水之瀾與日月之必照以觀之，抑何以知之哉？何則？流而為川、瀦而為海者，水也；人知水之混混，而不知其有本也。故觀水之術，不於歸會之所，必於湍急之處，則知其往過來續，而非朝滿夕除也；不舍晝夜，而非涸可立待也。觀水之瀾，則知其源之有本如此。若夫聖人之道，發而為小德川流、無時不然者，必有大德敦化者為之本焉。懸象於天、代明晝夜者，日月也；人知日月之有明，而不知其有本也。故觀日月之術，不於物無遁形之間，必於容光必照之處，則知其罅隙不遺，而非明此暗彼也；無幽不燭，而非大及小遺也。觀日月於容光之隙無不照，則知其明之有本如此。若夫聖人之道，用而為泛應曲當、無物不有者，必有一理渾然者為之本焉。然則聖道之大，豈徒然而已哉？抑嘗論之：聖人
translation_en:
…is not to be found anywhere else in the entire examination hall.

Examiner and Instructor Wu comments: In this exposition on the Mencius, the diction and spirit burst forth with elegance—is this not what is meant by "striving only to cast off hackneyed expressions, how arduous a task it is!"?

When the great worthy draws upon physical things to elucidate the Way of the Sages, he necessarily discerns its fundamental source through its manifest functioning. Now, as for the Way of the Sages, its functioning is easy to see, whereas its fundamental source is difficult to know. If one does not observe it by turning to therippling waves of water and the unfailing illumination of the sun and moon, how then could one come to know it?

Why is this so? That which flows forth to become rivers and gathers to become seas is water; people know the gushing abundance of water, yet do not know that it has a fundamental source. Therefore, the art of observing water lies not in looking at the places where it converges and gathers, but necesariamente in looking at the places where its current is swift and turbulent. Then one knows that as the past flows by, what follows continues unbroken, and it is not something that fills in the morning only to be drained by evening; it flows on without ceasing day and night, and is not something whose drying up can be expected at any moment. By observing the turbulent waves of water, one thus knows that its spring has a fundamental source such as this. In the same manner, when the Way of the Sages issues forth as lesser virtues flowing like river currents, never ceasing at any moment, there must be great virtue fostering universal transformation serving as its fundamental source.

That which hangs its images in the heavens and alternates in illuminating day and night is the sun and moon; people know that the sun and moon possess brightness, yet do not know that this brightness has a fundamental source. Therefore, the art of observing the sun and moon lies not in looking where myriad things have no way to hide their forms, but necessarily in looking at places where even the smallest chink admitting light is unfailingly illuminated. Then one knows that no crevice is overlooked, and it does not brighten this while leaving that in darkness; no hidden recess goes unlit, and it does not reach the great while neglecting the small. By observing that the sun and moon leave no chink unilluminated where light can enter, one thus knows that their brightness has a fundamental source such as this. In the same manner, when the Way of the Sages functions so as to respond broadly and suit every particular circumstance, present in all things without exception, there must be a single, all-encompassing principle in undifferentiated completeness serving as its fundamental source.

If this is so, how could the greatness of the Way of the Sages be merely accidental? Moreover, I have ventured to discuss it thus: the Sage…

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
即天地也天地之道其本不可知必觀其發為化育
流行者而後知聖人之道其本不可見必觀其發為
功用顯著者而後見故孔子賛堯舜必指其文章治
化而言詩書稱文武亦以其謨訓功烈而言至門人
記孔子亦備錄其容色言動以示人無乃皆欲人於
其用處驗其本歟後之學聖道者宜於此求焉
易義
后以財成天地之道輔相天地之宜以左右民
初九拔茅茹以其彙征吉
===
方湜
同考試官教諭劉批此題象言財成輔相所謂
賛天地之化育而與天地參聖人大有為之事也
爻言三陽在下相連而進拔茅連茹之象征行之
吉也占者陽剛則其征吉矣場中作者多昧本義
之旨此篇暢達不窘其庶幾善究易理者歟
考試官教諭劉批易義發明無遺佳作也
考試官教諭吳批易義詞理俱備初場得之
象言君道有為之極爻言陽剛類進之占夫時之泰
punctuated:
即天地也。天地之道，其本不可知，必觀其發為化育流行者而後知；聖人之道，其本不可見，必觀其發為功用顯著者而後見。故孔子賛堯、舜，必指其文章治化而言；《詩》、《書》稱文、武，亦以其謨訓功烈而言；至門人記孔子，亦備錄其容色言動以示人。無乃皆欲人於其用處驗其本歟？後之學聖道者，宜於此求焉。

易義

后以財成天地之道，輔相天地之宜，以左右民。初九，拔茅茹，以其彙，征吉。

方湜

同考試官教諭劉批：此題象言財成輔相，所謂賛天地之化育而與天地參，聖人大有為之事也；爻言三陽在下，相連而進，拔茅連茹之象，征行之吉也。占者陽剛，則其征吉矣。場中作者多昧《本義》之旨，此篇暢達不窘，其庶幾善究易理者歟！

考試官教諭劉批：易義發明無遺，佳作也。

考試官教諭吳批：易義詞理俱備，初場得之。

象言君道有為之極，爻言陽剛類進之占。夫時之泰
translation_en:
…is none other than Heaven and Earth. As for the Way of Heaven and Earth, its fundamental source cannot be known directly; one can know it only by observing how it manifests as the flowing processes of transformation and nurture. As for the Way of the Sage, its fundamental source cannot be seen directly; one can see it only by observing how it manifests in illustrious achievements and functions. Therefore, when Confucius praised Yao and Shun, he invariably pointed to their cultural accomplishments and transformative governance; when the Book of Odes (Shi) and the Book of Documents (Shu) extolled King Wen and King Wu, they likewise spoke in terms of their counsels, instructions, and meritorious deeds; and when the disciples recorded the life of Confucius, they too fully documented his countenance, demeanor, words, and actions to show to others. Was all of this not intended to guide people to verify the fundamental source through its outward functions? Those in later times who study the Way of the Sage ought to seek it here.

Exposition on the Book of Changes (Yi yi)

"The sovereign, in harmony with this, fashions and completes the Way of Heaven and Earth, and assists the suitability of Heaven and Earth, in order to aid the people." "Nine at the beginning: Pulling up the cogon grass with its roots, along with its kind; going forward brings good fortune." [Hexagram 11, Tai (Peace)]

Fang Shi 方湜

Associate Examiner, Instructor Liu 劉, comments: In this topic, the Overall Image (Xiang) speaks of fashioning, completing, and assisting—what is meant by assisting in the transforming and nourishing powers of Heaven and Earth and forming a triad with them, which is the great, active undertaking of a sage. The Line Statement (Yao) speaks of the three yang lines below advancing in connection with one another, symbolized by pulling up cogon grass with its interconnected roots, whereby going forward brings good fortune. If the diviner possesses yang firmness, then his going forward will be auspicious. Most candidates in the examination compound were blind to the purport of the Original Meaning (Benyi), whereas this essay is fluent, expressive, and unconstrained—surely the work of one who is adept at investigating the principles of the Changes!

Examiner, Instructor Liu 劉, comments: The meaning of the Changes is elucidated without omission; a fine piece of work.

Examiner, Instructor Wu 吳, comments: In this exposition on the Changes, both diction and principle are complete; I obtained it in the first session.

The Overall Image speaks of the ultimate active achievement of the ruler's Way, while the Line Statement speaks of the prognostication of yang firmness advancing together with its kind. Now, when the times are at peace (Tai)…

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
而大有為則陽剛得以連類而進也聖人傳彖繫爻
安得不各極言之哉且泰之為卦乾天居下坤地居
上乃二氣交泰之象體斯象者果何如哉亦惟有為
以盡道耳是故氣化流行紛綸相續此天地之道或
有過也人君則財成之敦五典而庸五禮分四時而
奠四方干以制其過焉人物稟受時勢不同此天地
之宜或有不及也人君則輔相之立學校而明禮義
制田里而教樹畜于以補其不及焉人君之財成輔
相如此非有他也惟欲左右斯民俾復其賦受之性
===
導引斯民使遂其長養之天而已斯非君道有為之
極而何若夫泰之初九以陽來居於內正君子道長
之日遇此爻者果如何哉亦惟連類而上進耳是故
九二之爻同類之陽也初則與之相引而進有如拔
夫茅也其茹以彙而相連焉九三之爻同體之剛也
初則與之牽連而往有若茅之拔也其根以類而並
起焉初九類進之象如此征行之吉也占者陽剛則
其征也必得以行其道其吉也可知其往也必得以
遂其志其善也可見斯非陽剛類進之占而何抑論
punctuated: 而大有為，則陽剛得以連類而進也。聖人傳彖繫爻，安得不各極言之哉？且泰之為卦，乾天居下，坤地居上，乃二氣交泰之象。體斯象者，果何如哉？亦惟有為以盡道耳。是故氣化流行，紛綸相續，此天地之道或有過也，人君則財成之，敦五典而庸五禮，分四時而奠四方，干以制其過焉；人物稟受，時勢不同，此天地之宜或有不及也，人君則輔相之，立學校而明禮義，制田里而教樹畜，于以補其不及焉。人君之財成輔相如此，非有他也，惟欲左右斯民，俾復其賦受之性；導引斯民，使遂其長養之天而已。斯非君道有為之極而何？若夫泰之初九，以陽來居於內，正君子道長之日。遇此爻者，果如何哉？亦惟連類而上進耳。是故九二之爻，同類之陽也，初則與之相引而進，有如拔夫茅也，其茹以彙而相連焉；九三之爻，同體之剛也，初則與之牽連而往，有若茅之拔也，其根以類而並起焉。初九類進之象如此，征行之吉也。占者陽剛，則其征也必得以行其道，其吉也可知；其往也必得以遂其志，其善也可見。斯非陽剛類進之占而何？抑論
translation_en:
…and achieves great things, then the yang and firm are able to advance together with their kind. In transmitting the Commentary on the Decision and appending the line statements, how could the sages not speak of each to the utmost?

Moreover, as a hexagram, Tai (Peace) has Qian (Heaven) residing below and Kun (Earth) residing above, which is the image of the two vital forces interacting in harmony. For one who embodies this image, how indeed should he act? It is simply to act so as to fulfill the Way. Therefore, as the transformations of vital force flow forth and continue in intricate succession, the Way of Heaven and Earth may at times go to excess; the ruler then regulates and completes it—enforcing the Five Constant Virtues and employing the Five Rites, dividing the four seasons and settling the four quarters—thereby [reading 于 for 干] curbing its excesses. As humans and things receive their endowments under differing times and circumstances, the appropriateness of Heaven and Earth may at times fall short; the ruler then assists and furthers it—establishing schools to clarify ritual and righteousness, regulating fields and villages to teach planting and husbandry—thereby remedying its deficiencies. That the ruler regulates, completes, assists, and furthers in this manner is for no other reason than that he wishes to aid and support these people so that they may recover their endowed nature, and to guide and lead these people so that they may fulfill their heaven-ordained growth and nourishment. What is this if not the ultimate achievement of the ruler's Way?

As for the First Nine of Tai, with yang coming to reside within, it is precisely the day when the Way of the noble man is waxing. For one who encounters this line, how indeed should he act? It is simply to join with his kind and advance upward. Therefore, the line of the Second Nine is a yang of the same kind; the First draws together with it and advances, just like pulling up cogongrass, whose roots are connectedaccording to their class. The line of the Third Nine is a firm line of the same trigram body; the First links together with it and goes forward, just as when cogongrass is pulled up, its roots rise together according to their kind. Such is the image of the First Nine advancing with its kind; it is the auspiciousness of going forward to act. If the diviner is yang and firm, then in his going forward he will surely be able to practice his Way, and his auspiciousness can be known; in his advancing he will surely be able to fulfill his ambition, and his goodness can be seen. What is this if not the prognostication of the yang and firm advancing with their kind?

Yet if we discuss…

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
之時之未泰致之為難時之既泰保之尤難但致泰
則關天運保泰則賴人力當此之際財成輔相以左
右民則上有其君矣三陽在下相連而進則下有其
臣矣君臣慶會明良相逢世道通泰民物亨嘉誠千
載一時也愚何幸身逢其盛
易與天地準故能彌綸天地之道仰以觀於天
文俯以察於地理是故知幽明之故原始反
終故知死生之說精氣為物游魂為變是故
知鬼神之情狀與天地相似故不違知周乎
===
萬物而道濟天下故不過旁行而不流樂天
知命故不憂安土敦乎仁故能愛範圍天地
之化而不過曲成萬物而不遺通乎晝夜之
道而知故神无方而易无體
梁輝
同考試官教諭劉批此題言易書與天地準故能彌
綸其道而窮理盡性至命三節皆聖人用易之事場
中作者往往溺於陳腐破語雷同而講欠明潔此篇
超出倫輩可直一魁
punctuated:
之，時之未泰，致之為難；時之既泰，保之尤難。但致泰則關天運，保泰則賴人力。當此之際，財成輔相以左右民，則上有其君矣；三陽在下，相連而進，則下有其臣矣。君臣慶會，明良相逢，世道通泰，民物亨嘉，誠千載一時也。愚何幸身逢其盛！

「易與天地準，故能彌綸天地之道。仰以觀於天文，俯以察於地理，是故知幽明之故；原始反終，故知死生之說；精氣為物，游魂為變，是故知鬼神之情狀。與天地相似，故不違；知周乎萬物，而道濟天下，故不過；旁行而不流，樂天知命，故不憂；安土敦乎仁，故能愛。範圍天地之化而不過，曲成萬物而不遺，通乎晝夜之道而知，故神无方而易无體。」

梁輝
同考試官教諭劉批：此題言《易》書與天地準，故能彌綸其道；而窮理、盡性、至命三節，皆聖人用《易》之事。場中作者往往溺於陳腐，破語雷同，而講欠明潔。此篇超出倫輩，可直一魁。
translation_en:
… of this: when the age has not yet reached peace and prosperity (Tai), bringing it about is difficult; when the age has already reached peace and prosperity, preserving it is even more difficult. However, bringing about peace depends on the destiny of Heaven, whereas preserving peace relies on human effort. At this juncture, regulating and completing, assisting and furthering [the course of Heaven and Earth] so as to aid the people—above, there is such a ruler! The three yang lines below, connected with one another and advancing together—below, there are such ministers! Ruler and ministers rejoice in their meeting, an enlightened sovereign and worthy subjects encounter one another, the way of the world is in smooth harmony, and the people and all things flourish in excellence—truly a moment that comes once in a thousand years! How fortunate am I to witness this golden age in person!

"The Changes is on a par with Heaven and Earth; therefore, it can comprehensively bind and order the Dao of Heaven and Earth. Looking up, [the sage] contemplates the patterns of Heaven, and looking down, he examines the principles of Earth; therefore, he knows the causes of the dark and the bright. Tracing things back to their beginnings and following them to their ends, he therefore knows the explanation of life and death. Essence and qi form things, and the wandering soul produces change; therefore, he knows the conditions and appearances of ghosts and spirits. Because he resembles Heaven and Earth, he does not go contrary to them. His knowledge encompasses the myriad things, and his Dao brings aid to all under Heaven; therefore, he does not err. He acts in all directions without being carried away; he rejoices in Heaven and knows its decree, and therefore has no anxiety. He rests securely in his position and is earnest in benevolence, and therefore is able to love. He encompasses and regulates the transformations of Heaven and Earth without erring, and intricately completes the myriad things without leaving any out. He comprehends the Dao of day and night and knows it; therefore, the spirit has no spatial restriction and the Changes has no fixed form."

Liang Hui 梁輝
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Liu 劉: This topic states that the Book of Changes (Yi) is on a par with Heaven and Earth and thus can comprehensively bind and order their Dao; while the three sections on exhausting principle, fully developing nature, and reaching destiny all concern how the sage uses the Changes. Writers in the examination hall often sink into clichés, their opening statements (poyu) are all alike, and their expositions lack clarity and conciseness. This essay stands out above its peers and is worthy of taking first place in this Classic.

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
考試官敎諭劉批易理深奧非用力精到者
不能發其蘊此作得之
考試官敎諭吳批易義簡明有文當是作者
易書等乎造化故能贊其道而無遺聖人用乎易書
必欲造其極而無間盖易與天地準故能贊其道而
無遺也聖人用之以窮理盡性而至命豈不造其極
而無間哉大傳論易道之大意謂天之道陽而健也
易書卦爻具有天之道而與之齊地之道陰而順也
易書卦爻具有地之道而與之準惟其齊準故於天
===
地之道為能彌之使其渾然而無間綸之俾其粲然
而有條焉易道之大如此惟聖人也仰以易而觀天
文之晝夜上下俯以易而察地理之南北高深則知
其幽明之故矣推原人物之始所以生反要人物之
終所以死則知夫死生之說矣陰精陽氣聚而成物
神之伸也魂游魄降散而為變鬼之歸也又有以知
夫鬼神之情狀焉幽明死生鬼神皆陰陽之理聖人
以易而窮之非窮理之事乎若夫天地之道知仁而
已聖人之知仁則與天地相似而不違知似乎天足
punctuated:
考試官敎諭劉批：易理深奧，非用力精到者不能發其蘊，此作得之。
考試官敎諭吳批：易義簡明有文，當是作者。
易書等乎造化，故能贊其道而無遺；聖人用乎易書，必欲造其極而無間。盖《易》與天地準，故能贊其道而無遺也；聖人用之以窮理、盡性而至命，豈不造其極而無間哉？《大傳》論《易》道之大，意謂：天之道，陽而健也，易書卦爻具有天之道而與之齊；地之道，陰而順也，易書卦爻具有地之道而與之準。惟其齊準，故於天地之道，為能彌之使其渾然而無間，綸之俾其粲然而有條焉。《易》道之大如此。惟聖人也，仰以《易》而觀天文之晝夜上下，俯以《易》而察地理之南北高深，則知其幽明之故矣；推原人物之始所以生，反要人物之終所以死，則知夫死生之說矣；陰精陽氣，聚而成物，神之伸也，魂游魄降，散而為變，鬼之歸也，又有以知夫鬼神之情狀焉。幽明、死生、鬼神，皆陰陽之理，聖人以《易》而窮之，非窮理之事乎？若夫天地之道，知仁而已；聖人之知仁，則與天地相似而不違。知似乎天，足
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Liu: The principles of the Book of Changes (Yi) are profound and abstruse; unless one's effort is refined and thorough, one cannot bring forth their hidden depths. This composition has achieved it.
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Wu: The exposition of the meaning of the Changes is concise, clear, and well-written; he is truly a capable writer.
The Book of Changes is equal to the creative transformations of nature, and therefore it can assist their Way without leaving anything out; when the sage makes use of the Book of Changes, he necessarily seeks to reach the ultimate perfection without any gap. Indeed, because the Changes is on a par with Heaven and Earth, it can assist their Way without omission; when the sage uses it to exhaust principle, fully realize nature, and attain to destiny, does he not reach the ultimate perfection without any gap? When the Great Treatise (Dazhuan) discusses the greatness of the Way of the Changes, its meaning is that the Way of Heaven is yang and vigorous, and the hexagrams and lines of the Book of Changes possess the Way of Heaven and are equal to it; the Way of Earth is yin and compliant, and the hexagrams and lines of the Book of Changes possess the Way of Earth and are on a par with it. Precisely because it is equal to and on a par with them, with respect to the Way of Heaven and Earth it is able to bind it together so as to make it an undivided whole without gaps, and to order its threads so as to make it distinctly arrayed in coherent patterns. Such is the greatness of the Way of the Changes. Only the sage, looking up, uses the Changes to observe the celestial patterns of day and night, above and below, and looking down, uses the Changes to examine the terrestrial patterns of south and north, height and depth, and thereby knows the causes of the dark and the bright; tracing back to the beginning of humans and things and how they are born, and seeking out the end of humans and things and how they die, he thereby knows the explanation of life and death; the yin essence and yang vital force gather to form things—which is the expansion of the spirit (shen)—and the ethereal soul wanders away while the corporeal soul descends, dispersing to become change—which is the return of the ghost (gui)—and thus he also has the means to know the true condition and characteristics of ghosts and spirits. The dark and the bright, life and death, and ghosts and spirits are all principles of yin and yang; when the sage uses the Changes to exhaust them, is this not the work of exhausting principle? As for the Way of Heaven and Earth, it is nothing more than wisdom and benevolence; the wisdom and benevolence of the sage resemble Heaven and Earth and do not contravene them. When his wisdom resembles Heaven, it suffices…

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
以周乎萬物仁似乎地足以濟乎天下則知不過矣
知既旁行而不滯仁又不流於姑息則知仁不偏矣
由是樂乎天理又知天命故心無憂而知益深隨處
皆安而無不仁故物能愛而仁益篤曰仁曰知固有
之性也聖人以易而盡之非盡性之事乎至若天地
之化至無窮也聖人則範圍之而不過萬物之生至
不一也聖人則曲成之而不遺晝夜之道未易知也
聖人又有以兼知其妙默契其機焉夫然後可見至
神之無方變易之無體也天地萬物晝夜皆命之所
===
在也聖人用易以至之非至命之事而何哉抑攷之
說卦亦有曰窮理盡性以至於命盖此之窮理盡性
至命以聖人言乃用易之事彼之窮理盡性至命就
易書言乃作易之功所指雖殊其致一也吁易作於
聖人而亦用於聖人此聖人所以有功於易有功於
天下後世也歟
書義
至諴感神矧兹有苗禹拜昌言曰俞班師振旅
鄭鴻
punctuated:
以周乎萬物，仁似乎地，足以濟乎天下，則知不過矣。知既旁行而不滯，仁又不流於姑息，則知仁不偏矣。由是樂乎天理，又知天命，故心無憂而知益深；隨處皆安，而無不仁，故物能愛而仁益篤。曰仁曰知，固有之性也，聖人以《易》而盡之，非盡性之事乎？至若天地之化，至無窮也，聖人則範圍之而不過；萬物之生，至不一也，聖人則曲成之而不遺；晝夜之道，未易知也，聖人又有以兼知其妙、默契其機焉。夫然後可見至神之無方、變易之無體也。天地、萬物、晝夜，皆命之所在也，聖人用《易》以至之，非至命之事而何哉？抑攷之《說卦》，亦有曰「窮理盡性以至於命」。盖此之窮理、盡性、至命，以聖人言，乃用《易》之事；彼之窮理、盡性、至命，就《易》書言，乃作《易》之功。所指雖殊，其致一也。吁！《易》作於聖人，而亦用於聖人，此聖人所以有功於《易》，有功於天下後世也歟！

《書》義
「至諴感神，矧兹有苗。」禹拜昌言，曰：「俞。」班師振旅。
鄭鴻
translation_en:
…to encompass the myriad things, and his benevolence resembles the earth, sufficient to bring aid to all under heaven; thus his wisdom does not err by excess. Since his wisdom operates on all sides without stagnation, and his benevolence does not lapse into mere indulgence, his wisdom and benevolence are free from partiality. Thereby he rejoices in the Principle of Heaven and also understands the Mandate of Heaven, so his mind has no anxiety and his wisdom grows ever deeper; in every circumstance he is at peace and never lacks benevolence, so he is able to love all creatures and his benevolence grows ever more sincere. What are called benevolence and wisdom are the inherent nature; when the sage fulfills them by means of the Changes (Yi), is this not the work of fulfilling one's nature to the utmost?

As for the transformations of heaven and earth, they are utterly inexhaustible, yet the sage casts and molds them so that they do not go to excess; the generation of the myriad things is utterly diverse, yet the sage brings them to intricate completion so that none is left out; the Way of day and night is not easy to know, yet the sage is further able to comprehend its subtleties altogether and silently accord with its subtle mechanisms. Only then can one see that supreme spirit has no fixed direction and that change and transformation have no fixed form. Heaven and earth, the myriad things, and day and night are all wherein the Mandate resides; when the sage uses the Changes to reach it, what is this if not the work of reaching the Mandate?

Moreover, if we examine the "Explanation of the Trigrams" (Shuogua), it also says: "Exhausting principle and fulfilling nature to the utmost, so as to reach the Mandate." Now, exhausting principle, fulfilling nature, and reaching the Mandate here are spoken of with respect to the sage, and refer to the work of using the Changes; exhausting principle, fulfilling nature, and reaching the Mandate there are spoken of with respect to the Book of Changes itself, and refer to the achievement of composing the Changes. Although what they point to differs, their ultimate import is one. Ah! The Changes was composed by the sage, and is also used by the sage—is this not how the sage has rendered service to the Changes, and rendered service to all under heaven and to future generations?

Exposition on the Book of Documents (Shu):
"Utmost sincerity moves the spirits; how much more this ruler of the Miao!" Yu bowed to thesplendid words and said, "Yes!" Thereupon he led back the army and arrayed the troops in triumph.
Zheng Hong 鄭鴻

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭李批此篇作者多不能形容禹
益一時氣象此作得之所宜錄出
考試官教諭劉批禹謨一篇詞理俱優故表出之
考試官教諭吳批此作有雍容氣象可取
同列言誠能感神而遠人不足化大臣即歆然其言
而威武不復施夫至誠之道神且感格況於人乎大
禹聞益之贊遂從而弛其威武焉其一德一心可見
矣思昔苗民逆命益贊于禹而推言及此意謂真實
無妄曰誠誠能感物曰誠彼神至幽而莫測至誠則
===
可以感之神至隱而難度至誠則可以格之況有苗
亦人耳雖曰反道敗德而良心固在也豈有感之不
應而事於征伐乎雖曰侮慢自賢而善性猶存也豈
有綏之不來而煩於兵力乎伯益之贊如此禹也乃
拜以致其敬俞以然其言拜非貌恭也敬盛德之言
而屈已受善也俞非面從也契至誠之道而舍已從
人也不惟拜之而遂還師於有苗之國威不復施矣
不惟俞之而且整旅於京師之地武不復用矣其應
之之速也若江河之決其從之之易也如形影之隨
punctuated:
同考試官教諭李批：此篇作者多不能形容禹、益一時氣象，此作得之，所宜錄出。
考試官教諭劉批：《禹謨》一篇，詞理俱優，故表出之。
考試官教諭吳批：此作有雍容氣象，可取。
同列言誠能感神而遠人不足化，大臣即歆然其言，而威武不復施。夫至誠之道，神且感格，況於人乎？大禹聞益之贊，遂從而弛其威武焉，其一德一心可見矣。思昔苗民逆命，益贊于禹而推言及此，意謂真實無妄曰誠，誠能感物曰誠。彼神至幽而莫測，至誠則可以感之；神至隱而難度，至誠則可以格之。況有苗亦人耳，雖曰反道敗德，而良心固在也，豈有感之不應，而事於征伐乎？雖曰侮慢自賢，而善性猶存也，豈有綏之不來，而煩於兵力乎？伯益之贊如此。禹也，乃拜以致其敬，俞以然其言。拜非貌恭也，敬盛德之言，而屈已受善也；俞非面從也，契至誠之道，而舍已從人也。不惟拜之，而遂還師於有苗之國，威不復施矣；不惟俞之，而且整旅於京師之地，武不復用矣。其應之之速也，若江河之決；其從之之易也，如形影之隨。
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Li: "Most writers on this topic fail to capture the spirit of Yu and Yi at that moment. This piece achieves it, and ought to be selected for publication."
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Liu: "This essay on the 'Counsels of Yu' excels in both diction and reasoning, so we have singled it out."
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Wu: "This piece has a poised and dignified air; it is worthy of selection."
When a colleague spoke of how utmost sincerity can move even the spirits, so that distant peoples are not difficult to transform, the great minister immediately delighted in and approved of his words, and martial force was no longer applied. Indeed, through the Way of utmost sincerity, even the spirits are moved and reached—how much more so human beings? When the Great Yu heard the counsel of Yi, he accordingly followed it and relaxed his martial force; their unity of virtue and unity of mind can thus be seen. Reflect on how in antiquity, when the Miao people defied commands, Yi assisted Yu and extended his reasoning to this point. His meaning was that being true, real, and free of falsehood is called sincerity, and that sincerity being able to move things is also called sincerity. Those spirits are most幽dark and unfathomable, yet utmost sincerity can move them; the spirits are most hidden and difficult to measure, yet utmost sincerity can reach them. How much more so the ruler of Miao, who is merely a human being! Although he is said to violate the Way and ruin virtue, his innate good conscience assuredly remains; how could it be that when moved he would not respond, making it necessary to engage in punitive expeditions? Although he is said to be insolent and self-righteous, his good nature still survives; how could it be that when pacified he would not come in submission, making it necessary to trouble with military force? Such was the counsel of Boyi. As for Yu, he then bowed to express his respect and said "Yes!" to affirm his words. His bowing was not mere outward politeness; he revered words of abundant virtue and humbled himself to accept what was good. His saying "Yes!" was not mere superficial compliance; he tallied with the Way of utmost sincerity and set aside his own views to follow others. Not only did he bow to him, he thereupon withdrew the army from the state of the Miao, and awe-inspiring force was no longer applied; not only did he say "Yes!" to him, he moreover marshaled the troops back in the capital region, and military might was no longer used. The swiftness of his response was like the bursting forth of the Jiang and the He rivers; the ease of his compliance was like a shadow following a form. …

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
大禹樂善之誠夫豈有彼此之間哉嗟夫禹之征苗
奉辭伐罪欲示以威武也益之賛禹推極至理欲專
尚德化也禹遂從而班師自後世觀之益之言若迂
而不切禹之舉若懦而無勇卒之帝乃誕敷文德舞
干羽于兩階而苗自格焉是武不足以威苗而德誠
可以感人譬之春風流暢寒谷草木自皆發榮也非
有虞德教之盛惡可語此哉
越三日庚戌太保乃以庶殷攻位于洛汭越五
日甲寅位成若翼日乙卯周公朝至于洛則
===
達觀于新邑營越三日丁巳用牲于郊牛二
越翼日戊午乃社于新邑牛一羊一豕一
梁金
同考試官教諭李批召誥一題本史臣紀事之辭
作者貴切實條暢此作可嘉
考試官教諭劉批此篇於召公得民周公告
神處有發明
考試官教諭吳批行文典雅宜錄之
史臣既紀日以見大臣定都而得民成其位復紀日
punctuated:
大禹樂善之誠，夫豈有彼此之間哉！嗟夫！禹之征苗，奉辭伐罪，欲示以威武也；益之賛禹，推極至理，欲專尚德化也；禹遂從而班師。自後世觀之，益之言若迂而不切，禹之舉若懦而無勇；卒之，帝乃誕敷文德，舞干羽于兩階，而苗自格焉。是武不足以威苗，而德誠可以感人，譬之春風流暢，寒谷草木自皆發榮也。非有虞德教之盛，惡可語此哉！

越三日庚戌，太保乃以庶殷攻位于洛汭，越五日甲寅，位成。若翼日乙卯，周公朝至于洛，則達觀于新邑營。越三日丁巳，用牲于郊，牛二。越翼日戊午，乃社于新邑，牛一、羊一、豕一。
梁金
同考試官教諭李批：召誥一題，本史臣紀事之辭，作者貴切實條暢，此作可嘉。
考試官教諭劉批：此篇於召公得民、周公告神處，有發明。
考試官教諭吳批：行文典雅，宜錄之。

史臣既紀日以見大臣定都而得民成其位，復紀日
translation_en:
… In the sincerity with which Great Yu delighted in goodness, how could there be any separation between oneself and others? Alas! When Yu went on the expedition against the Miao, he carried out the mandate to punish the guilty, wishing to display martial majesty; when Yi assisted Yu with his counsel, he deduced the ultimate principle, wishing to rely exclusively on moral transformation; and Yu thereupon followed him and withdrew his troops. Viewed from later generations, Yi's words might seem迂闊 (impractical) and wide of the mark, and Yu's action might seem timid and lacking in courage. Yet in the end, the Emperor widely diffused civil virtue, performing the shield-and-feather dance between the two staircases, and the Miao came to submit of their own accord. This shows that martial force was insufficient to overawe the Miao, whereas virtue could truly move people—just as when the spring breeze flows freely, the grasses and trees in a cold valley naturally all burst into bloom. Without the flourishing of moral teaching under the Lord of Yu [Shun], how could one speak of this?

"After three days, on the gengxu day, the Grand Protector led the multitude of Yin to lay out the sites at the bend of the Luo River. After five days, on the jiayin day, the sites were completed. On the next day, yimao, the Duke of Zhou arrived at Luo in the morning and thoroughly inspected the layout of the new city. After three days, on the dingsi day, he offered victims in the suburban sacrifice: two bulls. On the next day, wuwu, he offered sacrifice to the altars of the soil and grain in the new city: one bull, one sheep, and one pig."
Liang Jin 梁金
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Li: This topic from the "Announcement of the Duke of Shao" (Shao gao) is originally the narrative wording of a court historian. In writing on it, one values being concrete, accurate, and well-ordered and fluent; this composition is commendable.
Comment by Examiner Instructor Liu: This essay brings out new insights regarding how the Duke of Shao won the people and how the Duke of Zhou announced the work to the spirits.
Comment by Examiner Instructor Wu: The style of writing is classical and elegant; it is fitting to record it.

The court historian, having recorded the days to show how the great minister established the capital and won the people's service to complete its sites, again recorded the days…

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
以見聖臣相都而告神備其禮盖召公之定都率民
以攻位而位成周公之觀洛舉祀以告神而禮備史
臣得不詳紀之哉昔周成王因武王之志成宅中之
業召公經理於先周公相成於後故史臣紀之曰越
三日庚戌大保乃以庶殷攻位于洛汭盖以畿內之
民不征其力四方之民又未至洛故用遷洛之殷民
闢荆棘平高下以定其城郭宗廟郊社朝市之位焉
越五日甲寅位成則庶殷之趨事咸勤召公之使民
咸悅而前朝後市左祖右社之位成焉此召公之定
===
都然也若翼日乙卯之朝周公以上相之尊行視洛
之事路車乘馬聿來新邑衮衣繡裳至止洛汭則凡
召公經營之位曰城郭曰宗廟無不徧而觀之曰郊
社曰朝市無不周而覽之尤以作洛重事不可不告
乎神故越三日丁巳用牲于郊而牲用牛二者於尊
以簡為誠也越翼日戊午乃社于新邑而牲用牛一
羊一豕一者於卑以豐為貴也郊社之祭皆告以營
洛之事此周公之相都然也噫召公之攻位位成有
以得乎民周公之至洛觀位有以告乎神神人協相
punctuated: 以見聖臣相都而告神備其禮。盖召公之定都，率民以攻位而位成；周公之觀洛，舉祀以告神而禮備，史臣得不詳紀之哉？昔周成王因武王之志，成宅中之業，召公經理於先，周公相成於後，故史臣紀之曰：越三日庚戌，大保乃以庶殷攻位于洛汭。盖以畿內之民不征其力，四方之民又未至洛，故用遷洛之殷民，闢荆棘，平高下，以定其城郭、宗廟、郊社、朝市之位焉。越五日甲寅，位成，則庶殷之趨事咸勤，召公之使民咸悅，而前朝後市、左祖右社之位成焉。此召公之定都然也。若翼日乙卯之朝，周公以上相之尊，行視洛之事，路車乘馬，聿來新邑；衮衣繡裳，至止洛汭。則凡召公經營之位，曰城郭，曰宗廟，無不徧而觀之；曰郊社，曰朝市，無不周而覽之。尤以作洛重事，不可不告乎神，故越三日丁巳，用牲于郊，而牲用牛二者，於尊以簡為誠也；越翼日戊午，乃社于新邑，而牲用牛一、羊一、豕一者，於卑以豐為貴也。郊社之祭，皆告以營洛之事，此周公之相都然也。噫！召公之攻位、位成，有以得乎民；周公之至洛、觀位，有以告乎神。神人協相，
translation_en:
… to show how the sage minister inspected the capital, announced it to the spirits, and completed the rites. For in establishing the capital, the Duke of Shao (Shao Gong 召公) led the people to work on the sites until the sites were completed; and in inspecting Luo, the Duke of Zhou (Zhou Gong 周公) performed the sacrifices to announce it to the spirits until the rites were complete. How could the court historian fail to record this in detail?

In antiquity, King Cheng of Zhou (Zhou Chengwang 周成王), following the ambition of King Wu (Wuwang 武王), accomplished the enterprise of taking up residence at the center of the realm. The Duke of Shao planned and managed it beforehand, and the Duke of Zhou assisted in completing it afterward. Thus the historian recorded: On the third day, gengxu, the Grand Protector (Taibao 大保) led the multitude of Yin to work on the sites at the bend of the Luo River. This was because he did not conscript the labor of the people within the royal domain, and the people of the four quarters had not yet arrived at Luo; therefore, he employed the Yin people who had been relocated to Luo to clear away the brambles and level the high and low ground, so as to fix the sites for the inner and outer city walls, the ancestral temple, the altars of heaven and the soil, the court, and the market. On the fifth day, jiayin, the sites were completed. Thus the multitude of Yin all hastened to their tasks with diligence, and the Duke of Shao employed the people to their universal delight, so that the sites—with the court in front and the market behind, the ancestral temple on the left and the altar of the soil on the right—were completed. Such was the Duke of Shao's establishment of the capital.

As for the morning of the next day, yimao, the Duke of Zhou, with the exalted status of Senior Prime Minister, carried out the task of inspecting Luo. With state carriage and team of horses, he came to the new city; in dragon robe and embroidered skirt, he arrived at the bend of the Luo River. Then, of all the sites planned and laid out by the Duke of Shao—whether the city walls or the ancestral temple—there were none he did not inspect thoroughly; whether the altars of heaven and the soil or the court and the market, there were none he did not survey completely. Moreover, considering that the construction of Luo was a weighty affair that could not go unannounced to the spirits, on the third day, dingsi, he offered victims at the suburban altar. That he used two bulls for the victims was because, toward the exalted, simplicity is taken as sincerity. On the next day, wuwu, he sacrificed to the altar of the soil in the new city. That he used one bull, one sheep, and one pig for the victims was because, toward the lowly, abundance is valued. Both the suburban sacrifice and the sacrifice to the altar of the soil announced the affair of constructing Luo. Such was the Duke of Zhou's inspection of the capital.

Alas! Through working on the sites and completing them, the Duke of Shao was able to win the hearts of the people; through arriving at Luo and inspecting the sites, the Duke of Zhou was able to make announcement to the spirits. With spirits and men mutually assisting…

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
則定宅于洛豈非萬億年敬天之休歟抑考洛誥言
予惟乙卯朝至于洛卜宅此不言者召公於戊申已
卜周公之吉卜不殊乎召公之吉卜周召一心也成
王至豐告廟此不言者蓋成王於豐已告成王之告
祭無異乎周公之告祭君臣一體也有周君臣同心
同德若是其致雍熈泰和之治宜矣
詩義
鳳凰于飛翽翽其羽亦集爰止藹藹王多吉士
維君子使媚于天子鳳凰于飛翽翽其羽亦
===
傅于天藹藹王多吉人維君子命媚于庶人
鳳凰鳴矣于彼高岡梧桐生矣于彼朝陽
梁瑜
同考試官教諭張批召康公極言用賢之效與
賢不輕用之意欲成王之銳志於用賢也此作能
發之
考試官教諭劉批古以鳳凰喻賢才所以致
其愛重欲人君之尊禮之耳召康公凡三言之其
意蓋如此場中往往妄說此作能推原其意而
punctuated:
則定宅于洛，豈非萬億年敬天之休歟？抑考《洛誥》言：「予惟乙卯，朝至于洛，卜宅。」此不言者，召公於戊申已卜，周公之吉卜不殊乎召公之吉卜，周、召一心也。成王至豐告廟，此不言者，蓋成王於豐已告，成王之告祭無異乎周公之告祭，君臣一體也。有周君臣同心同德若是，其致雍熈泰和之治宜矣。

詩義
鳳凰于飛，翽翽其羽，亦集爰止。藹藹王多吉士，維君子使，媚于天子。鳳凰于飛，翽翽其羽，亦傅于天。藹藹王多吉人，維君子命，媚于庶人。鳳凰鳴矣，于彼高岡。梧桐生矣，于彼朝陽。
梁瑜
同考試官教諭張批：召康公極言用賢之效與賢不輕用之意，欲成王之銳志於用賢也。此作能發之。
考試官教諭劉批：古以鳳凰喻賢才，所以致其愛重，欲人君之尊禮之耳。召康公凡三言之，其意蓋如此。場中往往妄說，此作能推原其意，而
translation_en:
… then fixing the royal residence at Luo—was this not a blessing of revering Heaven for ten thousand times a hundred million years? Furthermore, if we examine the "Announcement Concerning Luo" (Luo gao), it says: "On the day yimao, in the morning I came to Luo and divined about the residence." That it is not mentioned here is because the Duke of Shao had already divined on the day wushen; the auspicious divination of the Duke of Zhou did not differ from the auspicious divination of the Duke of Shao, for the Dukes of Zhou and Shao were of one mind. That King Cheng went to Feng to announce it to the ancestral temple is also not mentioned here because King Cheng had already made the announcement at Feng; the sacrificial announcement of King Cheng was no different from the sacrificial announcement of the Duke of Zhou, for ruler and minister formed a single body. Since the ruler and ministers of the Zhou dynasty were of one heart and one virtue like this, it was only fitting that they brought about an era of harmonious and resplendent peace.

Expositions on the Classic of Poetry (Shi yi)

"The male and female phoenixes go flying, rustling are their wings, and they gather where they rest. Numerous are the King's many fine officers; it is the lord who employs them, and they show love and devotion to the Son of Heaven. The male and female phoenixes go flying, rustling are their wings, and they soar up to heaven. Numerous are the King's many fine men; it is the lord who commands them, and they show love and kindness to the common people. The male and female phoenixes sing out, on that high ridge. The parasol trees grow, on that eastern slope facing the morning sun."

Liang Yu 梁瑜

Comment (pi) by Associate Examiner (tong kaoshiguan), County Instructor (jiaoyu) Zhang: Duke Kang of Shao (Shao Kanggong) spoke to the utmost of the efficacy of employing worthy men and the idea that worthy men do not lightly allow themselves to be employed, wishing to make King Cheng earnestly determined to employ the worthy. This composition is able to bring this out.

Comment by Examiner (kaoshiguan), County Instructor Liu: In antiquity, the phoenix was used as a metaphor for worthy talent in order to express deep affection and esteem for them, wishing only that the ruler of men would honor and treat them with ritual courtesy. Duke Kang of Shao spoke of it three times in all, and his meaning was precisely this. In the examination compound, candidates often make wild assertions, but this composition is able to trace the original meaning, and…

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
文足以發之真佳士也
考試官教諭吳批此篇言用賢為致福之由
深得其旨
既與賢才盛而必效忠愛之誠復喻賢才出而必際
明良之會夫賢才者致治之具也大臣之告君安得
不言其用而效忠愛之誠出而際明良之會哉昔召
康公從成王游歌而作詩既極言夫福祿之盛此則
告以致福祿之由而因時鳳凰至故托以起興若曰
鳳凰之飛羽聲之有聞則既覽德輝而下之而止其
===
所矣此藹藹然賢才之羣集莫非有憑有翼之士委
質于君而君使之其必脩政立事而上有以愛乎君
焉愛非諂諛一皆忠誠之所發也繼又興之若曰鳳
凰之飛羽聲之翽翽則既翔于千仞之表而傅于天
矣此藹藹然賢才之眾多莫非有孝有德之人委身
于君而君命之其必敷化善俗而下有以愛乎民焉
愛非狎侮一皆德意之所形也所謂賢才盛而必效
忠愛之誠者如此然鳳凰非梧桐不棲猶賢者非明
君不仕故又托以比之若曰鳳凰之鳴其聲為甚和
punctuated:
文足以發之，真佳士也。
考試官教諭吳批：此篇言用賢為致福之由，深得其旨。
既興賢才盛而必效忠愛之誠，復喻賢才出而必際明良之會。夫賢才者，致治之具也。大臣之告君，安得不言其用而效忠愛之誠、出而際明良之會哉？昔召康公從成王游歌而作詩，既極言夫福祿之盛，此則告以致福祿之由，而因時鳳凰至，故托以起興。若曰：鳳凰之飛，羽聲之有聞，則既覽德輝而下之，而止其所矣；此藹藹然賢才之羣集，莫非有憑有翼之士，委質于君，而君使之，其必脩政立事，而上有以愛乎君焉，愛非諂諛，一皆忠誠之所發也。繼又興之，若曰：鳳凰之飛，羽聲之翽翽，則既翔于千仞之表，而傅于天矣；此藹藹然賢才之眾多，莫非有孝有德之人，委身于君，而君命之，其必敷化善俗，而下有以愛乎民焉，愛非狎侮，一皆德意之所形也。所謂賢才盛而必效忠愛之誠者如此。然鳳凰非梧桐不棲，猶賢者非明君不仕，故又托以比之。若曰：鳳凰之鳴，其聲為甚和…
translation_en:
… and his prose is equal to giving expression to it. Truly a fine scholar!

Comment by Examiner Wu, Instructor (jiaoyu): This essay explains that employing worthy talent is the means of bringing about blessings, deeply grasping the purport of the passage.

Having first used an evocative image [read 興 for 與] to show that when worthy talents flourish they will surely offer the sincerity of loyalty and love, the poet then uses a metaphor to show that when worthy talents come forth they will surely meet with a conjuncture of an enlightened ruler and fine ministers. Now, worthy talents are the instruments for bringing about good order. When a great minister counsels his ruler, how could he fail to speak of how, when employed, they offer the sincerity of loyalty and love, and how, in coming forth, they meet with a conjuncture of an enlightened ruler and fine ministers? In antiquity, when Duke Kang of Shao (Shao Kanggong 召康公) accompanied King Cheng (Cheng Wang 成王) on an excursion, he sang and composed this ode ("Juan'e" 卷阿). Having spoken to the utmost of the abundance of blessings and dignities, here he informs the king of the means by which blessings and dignities are brought about; and because phoenixes happened to arrive at that time, he borrowed them to initiate an evocative image. It is as if he said: When the phoenixes fly, the sound of their wings is heard, for they have beheld the radiance of virtue, descended to it, and come to rest in their proper place; so too, this thriving multitude of worthy talents gathered together are none other than gentlemen who can be relied upon and who can give support. Having pledged themselves in service to the ruler, when the ruler employs them, they will surely cultivate government and establish achievements, and thus above have the means to love their ruler—a love that is not flattery, but is wholly an expression of loyal sincerity. Next he again uses an evocative image, as if to say: When the phoenixes fly, with the rustling sound of their wings, they have soared beyond a thousand fathoms and reached up to heaven; so too, this thriving multitude of numerous worthy talents are none other than men of filial piety and virtue. Having devoted themselves to the ruler, when the ruler gives them his commands, they will surely spread transforming teaching and improve customs, and thus below have the means to love the people—a love that is not familiar or disrespectful, but is wholly a manifestation of virtuous intentions. Such is what is meant by saying that when worthy talents flourish, they will surely offer the sincerity of loyalty and love. Yet just as the phoenix does not roost save on the wutong tree, so a worthy man does not take office save under an enlightened ruler; therefore the poet further borrows this to make a comparison. It is as if he said: When the phoenixes sing, their voices are most harmonious…

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
也然不於其他而必於高岡之上豈不猶賢者之在
高世而懷抱負之大乎梧桐之生其勢為甚盛也然
不於其他而必於朝陽之地豈不猶賢君之居治朝
而享德業之成乎有治朝之賢君而後高世之賢才
樂用有朝陽之梧桐而後高岡之鳳凰來鳴所謂賢
才出而必際明良之會者如此吁明良相逢千載一
時康公以是而告成王欲其求賢以自輔而為致福
之本者何其至哉大抵泰和盛治固為可樂而亦可
戒康公言求賢之道而反覆於鳳凰以鳳凰希世之
===
物欲成王之有所感也成王能勉以求之則泰和盛
治可以長保於無窮矣然則康公其亦當時之鳳凰
也歟
學有緝熈于光明
劉實
同考試官教諭張批
考試官教諭劉批此題場中皆以學至于光
明為造其極不知所謂極者何物蓋光明本非
外来乃吾心之本體也學而明之繼續不已則
punctuated:
也，然不於其他而必於高岡之上，豈不猶賢者之在高世而懷抱負之大乎？梧桐之生，其勢為甚盛也，然不於其他而必於朝陽之地，豈不猶賢君之居治朝而享德業之成乎？有治朝之賢君，而後高世之賢才樂用；有朝陽之梧桐，而後高岡之鳳凰來鳴。所謂賢才出而必際明良之會者如此。吁！明良相逢，千載一時。康公以是而告成王，欲其求賢以自輔，而為致福之本者，何其至哉！大抵泰和盛治，固為可樂，而亦可戒。康公言求賢之道，而反覆於鳳凰，以鳳凰希世之物，欲成王之有所感也。成王能勉以求之，則泰和盛治，可以長保於無窮矣。然則康公其亦當時之鳳凰也歟！

學有緝熈于光明。
劉實
同考試官教諭張批：
考試官教諭劉批：此題場中皆以學至于光明為造其極，不知所謂極者何物。蓋光明本非外来，乃吾心之本體也。學而明之，繼續不已，則
translation_en:
… Yet it does not do so elsewhere, but necessarily atop a high ridge—is this not like a worthy standing lofty above the world and cherishing great aspirations? When the parasol tree (wutong) grows, its vigor is most flourishing; yet it does not do so elsewhere, but necessarily in a place facing the morning sun—is this not like a worthy ruler occupying a well-governed court and enjoying the accomplishment of virtuous deeds? Only when there is a worthy ruler in a well-governed court do talents who stand lofty above the world gladly accept employment; only when there is a parasol tree facing the morning sun does the phoenix on the high ridge come to sing. Such is what is meant by worthy talents emerging and necessarily encountering a juncture of an enlightened ruler and fine ministers. Ah! The meeting of an enlightened ruler and fine ministers happens once in a thousand years. Duke Kang (Kang gong 康公) spoke of this to admonish King Cheng (Cheng wang 成王), wishing him to seek out worthies to assist himself as the foundation for bringing about blessings—how consummate this was! In general, an era of supreme harmony and flourishing governance is certainly cause for joy, yet also cause for caution. In speaking of the way of seeking worthies, Duke Kang repeatedly dwelled upon the phoenix because the phoenix is a creature rare in the world, wishing King Cheng to be moved by it. If King Cheng could exert himself in seeking them, then supreme harmony and flourishing governance could long be preserved without end. If so, was not Duke Kang himself also a phoenix of that time!

"In learning, there is unceasing continuation unto bright illumination" (Xue you jixi yu guangming 學有緝熈于光明).
By Liu Shi 劉實.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Zhang 張: [blank]
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Liu 劉: On this topic, everyone in the examination hall took "learning reaching unto bright illumination" as attaining the ultimate, without knowing what this so-called "ultimate" actually is. For bright illumination does not originally come from outside; it is the original substance of our own mind. By learning and illuminating it, continuing without cease, then…

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
私欲浄盡有以復其心體之光明庶乎敬可及矣此
作能發之而結引緝熈敬止配說尤見筆力魁何忝
考試官教諭吳批學有緝熈于光明一題惟此
得旨當冠本房
賢君不自足而勉其當然不自已而復其本然夫欲
勉於學正其所以不自足也學焉而不自已則豈不
有以復其本然之光明而能敬哉昔成王受羣臣敬
天之戒而自為荅之之辭若曰我不聰而未能敬也
然願學焉惟日孳孳極深研幾而加格物致知之功
===
以敬脩其可願終日乾乾靜存動察而致誠意正心
之力以懋昭其大德此不自足而勉其當然也心德
本自光明而物欲蔽之故明者於是而有昧矣苟今
日新之而明日不繼則何以去物欲之蔽而致其明
乎必於格物致知益有以加其功而日日新之無少
間斷使光明者愈至於光明而此事有此理皆洞然
而明白可也心體本無昏昧而利欲交之故昏者不
復以有明矣苟今日明之而後日或輟則何以絕利
欲之交而復其明乎必於誠意正心而益有致其力
punctuated:
私欲浄盡，有以復其心體之光明，庶乎敬可及矣。此作能發之，而結引「緝熈敬止」配說，尤見筆力，魁何忝！
考試官教諭吳批：「學有緝熈于光明」一題，惟此得旨，當冠本房。
賢君不自足而勉其當然，不自已而復其本然。夫欲勉於學，正其所以不自足也。學焉而不自已，則豈不有以復其本然之光明而能敬哉？昔成王受羣臣敬天之戒，而自為荅之之辭，若曰：我不聰而未能敬也，然願學焉。惟日孳孳，極深研幾，而加格物致知之功，以敬脩其可願；終日乾乾，靜存動察，而致誠意正心之力，以懋昭其大德。此不自足而勉其當然也。心德本自光明，而物欲蔽之，故明者於是而有昧矣。苟今日新之而明日不繼，則何以去物欲之蔽而致其明乎？必於格物致知，益有以加其功，而日日新之，無少間斷，使光明者愈至於光明，而此事有此理，皆洞然而明白可也。心體本無昏昧，而利欲交之，故昏者不復以有明矣。苟今日明之而後日或輟，則何以絕利欲之交而復其明乎？必於誠意正心，而益有致其力，
translation_en:
…selfish desires are completely eliminated, and one has the means to restore the original brightness of the substance of the mind; then perhaps reverence can be attained! This essay succeeds in bringing out this point, and its conclusion—drawing on "continuing and brightening [his] reverent resting" as a counterpart—especially demonstrates the vigor of its brushwork. How could it be unworthy of first place?

Comment by Examiner Instructor Wu: On the topic "In learning there is a continuing and brightening unto glorious brightness," only this essay grasps the main purport; it should stand first in its examination ward.

A worthy ruler is not self-satisfied and thus exerts himself in what ought to be done; he does not cease of himself and thus restores his original nature. Now, his desire to exert himself in learning is precisely wherein he is not self-satisfied. If he learns and does not cease of himself, how could he fail to restore his original brightness and thus be capable of reverence? In ancient times, when King Cheng received the admonition of his ministers to revere Heaven, he composed words in reply, as if to say: "I am not perceptive and am not yet able to be reverent; yet I wish to learn. Only let me be diligent day by day, plumbing the depths and investigating the subtle springs of action, applying the effort of investigating things and extending knowledge so as to reverently cultivate what is desirable; let me be vigilant all day long, preserving my mind in stillness and examining it in activity, devoting my strength to making the intentions sincere and rectifying the mind so as to vigorously manifest great virtue." This was his not being self-satisfied and exerting himself in what ought to be done. The virtue of the mind is originally bright of itself, yet material desires obscure it, and thus what is bright thereupon becomes darkened. If one renews it today but fails to continue tomorrow, how can one remove the obscuration of material desires and bring about its brightness? Only by increasingly applying effort to investigating things and extending knowledge, renewing it day by day without the slightest interruption, so that what is bright attains ever greater brightness and the principle inherent in every affair becomes thoroughly clear and manifest—only then will it do. The substance of the mind is originally without dimness or obscurity, yet desires for profit交 [entangle/assail] it, and thus what is darkened no longer has the means to be bright. If one clarifies it today but perhaps stops on a later day, how can one sever the entanglement of desires for profit and restore its brightness? One must, in making the intentions sincere and rectifying the mind, increasingly devote one's strength…

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
而日日明之有所接續使昏昧者不復為昏昧而事
物有此理皆豁然而呈露可也此非不自已而復其
本然乎能如是則於其謂敬庶乎有所及矣抑論之
敬天有道顯學是也顯學有道緝熈是也周自文王
緝熈敬止而創業于其前成王緝熈光明而守成于
其後此所以成周家八百年之基業也德以敬而成
業以敬而著先儒謂敬者聖學之所以成始成終觀
此益信
春秋義
===
齊師宋師次于郎莊公十年齊人陳人曹人伐宋
莊公十四年叔孫州仇帥師墮郈季孫斯仲孫
何忌帥師墮費公圍成定公十二年
李昕
同考試官訓導陳批此題皆本傳註融會者
少是篇又塲中之表表者用宜錄出
同考試官教諭張批題意明白作者自不能
因此語彼往往詳於孔子而畧管仲之說忽得
此卷發明無餘書當快意讀易盡是之謂歟
punctuated:
而日日明之，有所接續，使昏昧者不復為昏昧，而事物有此理，皆豁然而呈露可也。此非不自已而復其本然乎？能如是，則於其謂敬，庶乎有所及矣。抑論之，敬天有道，顯學是也；顯學有道，緝熈是也。周自文王緝熈敬止而創業于其前，成王緝熈光明而守成于其後，此所以成周家八百年之基業也。德以敬而成，業以敬而著。先儒謂「敬者，聖學之所以成始成終」，觀此益信。

春秋義

齊師宋師次于郎〔莊公十年〕齊人陳人曹人伐宋〔莊公十四年〕叔孫州仇帥師墮郈季孫斯仲孫何忌帥師墮費公圍成〔定公十二年〕
李昕
同考試官訓導陳批：此題皆本傳註，融會者少。是篇又塲中之表表者，用宜錄出。
同考試官教諭張批：題意明白，作者自不能因此語彼，往往詳於孔子而畧管仲之說。忽得此卷，發明無餘。「書當快意讀易盡」，是之謂歟！
translation_en:
…and illuminate it day by day with continuous effort, causing what was darkened to be darkened no longer, so that the principle inherent in all affairs and things is openly revealed. Is this not ceaselessly striving to restore one's original nature? If one is able to do this, then one will come close to what is called reverence (jing). Furthermore, let us consider this: there is a Way to revere Heaven, and that is manifest learning; there is a Way to manifest learning, and that is continuous illumination (jixi). In the Zhou dynasty, from the time King Wen continuously illuminated his reverent resting place and founded the dynastic enterprise beforehand, to when King Cheng continuously illuminated what is bright and preserved the accomplishment afterward—this was how they established the eight-hundred-year foundational enterprise of the House of Zhou. Virtue is perfected through reverence, and the enterprise is made manifest through reverence. Former Confucian scholars said, "Reverence is that whereby sagely learning completes both its beginning and its end." Viewing this, one finds it even more credible.

Expositions on the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

"The armies of Qi and Song halted at Lang" [tenth year of Duke Zhuang]; "The men of Qi, Chen, and Cao invaded Song" [fourteenth year of Duke Zhuang]; "Shusun Zhouqiu led a force and demolished Hou; Jisun Si and Zhongsun Heji led a force and demolished Bi; the Duke besieged Cheng" [twelfth year of Duke Ding].
By Li Xin 李昕.
Associate Examiner Assistant Instructor (xundao) Chen comments: Responses to this topic are all based on the commentary and annotations, yet few manage to synthesize them thoroughly. This essay is an outstanding piece from the examination hall, and therefore ought to be selected for publication.
Associate Examiner Instructor (jiaoyu) Zhang comments: The meaning of the topic is clear, yet writers naturally fail to connect one part to the other, often elaborating on Confucius while neglecting the discussion of Guan Zhong 管仲. Suddenly coming across this paper, I find it elucidates the theme exhaustively. "When a book delights the mind, it is all too quickly read to the end"—is this not what is meant here!

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭劉批能發明題中微旨不至
穿鑿可取
考試官教諭吳批管仲相齊千載所稱聖人
用魯一時機會此篇發明殆盡熟於麟經者
兵政始失而終得由伯主用賢臣之未久國政始得
而終失由望國用聖人之未專此春秋於齊桓二役
有書師書人之異於我魯三邑有書墮書圍之殊盖
皆有其故也歟何則齊桓入國之初已得仲父而相
之矣未幾始因魯蓄長勺之憾於是連師于宋而為
===
于郎之次繼因宋忘北杏之好於是徵兵陳曹而為
討宋之行然春秋於二國次郎稱師者所以譏其不
撫其民輕用大衆也於三國伐宋稱人者所以著其
將卑師少以制用兵也用兵得失如此則將焉用管
仲之相哉按莊公九年小白入齊始因鮑叔之薦用
以為相然則次郎之役仲雖得政盖未久也自伐宋
之後終其身未嘗興大衆出侵伐未必不出於其功
也使桓公不能任之專且久則九合之功有未可望
尚何一役用師之足議哉故曰由伯主用之未久也
punctuated:
考試官教諭劉批：能發明題中微旨，不至穿鑿，可取。
考試官教諭吳批：管仲相齊，千載所稱；聖人用魯，一時機會。此篇發明殆盡，熟於《麟經》者。
兵政始失而終得，由伯主用賢臣之未久；國政始得而終失，由望國用聖人之未專。此《春秋》於齊桓二役，有書師、書人之異；於我魯三邑，有書墮、書圍之殊。盖皆有其故也歟？何則？齊桓入國之初，已得仲父而相之矣。未幾，始因魯蓄長勺之憾，於是連師于宋，而為于郎之次；繼因宋忘北杏之好，於是徵兵陳、曹，而為討宋之行。然《春秋》於二國次郎稱「師」者，所以譏其不撫其民，輕用大衆也；於三國伐宋稱「人」者，所以著其將卑師少，以制用兵也。用兵得失如此，則將焉用管仲之相哉？按莊公九年，小白入齊，始因鮑叔之薦，用以為相。然則次郎之役，仲雖得政，盖未久也。自伐宋之後，終其身未嘗興大衆出侵伐，未必不出於其功也。使桓公不能任之專且久，則九合之功有未可望，尚何一役用師之足議哉？故曰：由伯主用之未久也。
translation_en:
Examiner and Instructor Liu's comment: It is able to elucidate the subtle import within the topic without falling into forced interpretations; it is worthy of selection.

Examiner and Instructor Wu's comment: Guan Zhong's (管仲) serving as chief minister of Qi has been praised for a thousand years; the Sage's being employed in Lu was the opportunity of an era. This essay elucidates both almost exhaustively—the work of one thoroughly versed in the Unicorn Classic [the Spring and Autumn Annals].

That military administration was at first mishandled and ultimately mastered was because the hegemon had not yet employed his worthy minister for long; that state administration was at first mastered and ultimately lost was because a prestigious state did not employ the Sage with undivided authority. This is why the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), in the two campaigns of Duke Huan of Qi (齊桓公), differs in recording "army" (shi 師) and recording "men" (ren 人); and in the affair of the three cities of our state of Lu, differs in recording "dismantled" (hui 墮) and recording "besieged" (wei 圍). Surely there are reasons for all of these!

Why is this so? When Duke Huan of Qi first entered his state, he had already obtained Uncle Zhong [Guan Zhong] and made him chief minister. Before long, first because he harbored resentment against Lu over the battle of Changshao (長勺), he joined forces with Song and encamped at Lang (郎); subsequently, because Song forgot the amity of the covenant at Beixing (北杏), he requisitioned troops from Chen and Cao and undertook an expedition to punish Song. Yet in the two states' encamping at Lang, the Spring and Autumn Annals refers to them as "armies" in order to censure them for failing to soothe their people and lightly mobilizing large multitudes; whereas in the three states' attacking Song, it refers to them as "men" in order to make manifest that the commanders were of low rank and the troops few, thereby exercising restraint in the use of military force. With the successes and failures in the use of military force being such as this, what then was the use of having Guan Zhong as chief minister?

If we examine the record, in the ninth year of Duke Zhuang (莊公) [685 BCE], Xiaobai (小白) [Duke Huan] entered Qi and first employed Guan Zhong as chief minister on the recommendation of Bao Shu (鮑叔). That being so, at the time of the campaign of encamping at Lang [684 BCE], although Zhong had obtained the reins of government, it had in fact not yet been for long. From the attack on Song [681 BCE] onward, to the end of his life he never again mobilized large multitudes to go out on invasions or attacks—which was not necessarily not due to his merit. Had Duke Huan not been able to entrust him with authority both exclusively and for a long time, then the achievement of uniting the feudal lords nine times could not have been hoped for—how then would the mobilization of an army in a single campaign even be worth discussing? Therefore I say: it was because the hegemon had not yet employed him for long.

title: 成化十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
若夫定公即位以来已得孔子而用之矣未幾始因
吾夫子一言之重於是叔季感化各毀其邑公室曾
不動其聲色繼以公斂處父一言之惑於是孟孫方
命不肯墮邑我公遂躬駕而圍成然春秋前書叔孫
墮郈季孫墮費者所以喜先王之制復行也繼書公
圍成者所以著公室之威遽褻也政事得失若此則
亦何望聖人之用哉按是年孔子為魯司冠雖用事
未能專得魯國之政越明年方由大司冠攝相事與
聞國政然則圍成之役非必出吾夫子之意也使聖
===
人得志行乎魯東周之言可徵尚何一邑不墮之足
恤哉故曰由魯國用之未專也大抵春秋之世五伯
桓公為盛而一匡管仲有功然亦不過措世小康而
已獨惜吾夫子仕丁魯定不足與有成也使遇齊桓
以大有作為之資而告以仁義之說則師皆湯武之
師業為帝王之業而伯圖一轉可為王道尚何區區
取於管仲之功哉
同盟于戲襄公九年公至自伐鄭襄公十年同盟
于亳城北公至自伐鄭會于蕭魚公
punctuated:
若夫定公即位以来，已得孔子而用之矣。未幾，始因吾夫子一言之重，於是叔、季感化，各毀其邑，公室曾不動其聲色；繼以公斂處父一言之惑，於是孟孫方命不肯墮邑，我公遂躬駕而圍成。然《春秋》前書「叔孫墮郈」、「季孫墮費」者，所以喜先王之制復行也；繼書「公圍成」者，所以著公室之威遽褻也。政事得失若此，則亦何望聖人之用哉？按是年孔子為魯司冠，雖用事，未能專得魯國之政；越明年，方由大司冠攝相事，與聞國政。然則圍成之役，非必出吾夫子之意也。使聖人得志行乎魯，「東周」之言可徵，尚何一邑不墮之足恤哉？故曰：由魯國用之未專也。大抵春秋之世，五伯桓公為盛，而一匡管仲有功，然亦不過措世小康而已。獨惜吾夫子仕丁魯定，不足與有成也。使遇齊桓，以大有作為之資，而告以仁義之說，則師皆湯、武之師，業為帝王之業，而伯圖一轉可為王道，尚何區區取於管仲之功哉？
「同盟于戲」《襄公九年》、「公至自伐鄭」《襄公十年》、「同盟于亳城北，公至自伐鄭，會于蕭魚，公
translation_en:
As for Duke Ding of Lu (定公), since ascending the throne he had already obtained Confucius and employed him. Before long, initially because of the weight of a single word from our Master, the Shusun (叔孫) and Jisun (季孫) clans were moved and transformed, each dismantling the walls of their cities without the ducal house so much as raising its voice or changing its countenance. Subsequently, misled by a single word from Gonglian Chufu (公斂處父), the Mengsun (孟孫) clan defied orders and refused to dismantle its city walls, whereupon our Duke personally rode forth to besiege Cheng (成). Yet the reason the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) first recorded "Shusun dismantled Hou (郈)" and "Jisun dismantled Bi (費)" was to rejoice that the institutions of the former kings were once again being put into practice; and the reason it subsequently recorded "The Duke besieged Cheng" was to make manifest how the authority of the ducal house had suddenly been profaned. When the successes and failures of governance were like this, what hope could there be for the employment of a sage? Note that in this year Confucius was Minister of Crime (Sikou [written 司冠 for 司寇]) of Lu; although he handled affairs, he had not yet gained exclusive authority over the governance of the state of Lu. Only in the following year did he advance from Grand Minister of Crime (Da Sikou) to act as Prime Minister and participate in hearing state governance. This being so, the campaign to besiege Cheng did not necessarily stem from our Master's intention. Had the sage obtained his ambition to carry out his Way in Lu, his words about making an "Eastern Zhou" could have been realized—why then would a single city's failure to be dismantled have been worth worrying over? Therefore I say: it was because the state of Lu had not yet employed him with exclusive authority. On the whole, in the world of the Spring and Autumn period, among the Five Hegemons Duke Huan (桓公) was the most flourishing, and in uniting and rectifying the realm Guan Zhong (管仲) had merit; yet this amounted to nothing more than placing the world in a state of Lesser Tranquility (xiaokang). It is only to be regretted that our Master's service coincided with Duke Ding of Lu, who was inadequate for achieving great things together with him. Had he encountered Duke Huan of Qi, with his natural endowment for great accomplishments, and instructed him in the doctrines of benevolence and righteousness, then his armies would all have been the armies of Tang (湯) and Wu (武), his enterprise would have been the enterprise of Emperors and Kings, and at a single turn the hegemonic design could have become the Kingly Way—why then would he have taken mere petty satisfaction in the功 (merit) of Guan Zhong?
